out.other_title: Complexity model of debate: polynomial-time judge, computationally unbounded debaters
out.rationale: Irving et al. replace the human judge with a polynomial-time algorithm H and allow the models arbitrary computational power, with H answering questions directly corresponding to the class P; the authors start from the analogy this motivates (humans as polynomial-time Turing machines, models as computationally unbounded) and use it to argue that critiques are a particularly natural form of assistance. The extension is an argument, not a theorem.
out.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Complexity-theoretic justification for assistance schemes; holds only as an analogy, with humans as polynomial-time verifiers.

text: In Appendix B the authors argue that critiques are a particularly natural form of assistance from the perspective of proof systems, starting from the analogy motivated by [ICA18] between scalable oversight and interactive proof systems from complexity theory, with humans as analogous to polynomial-time Turing machines and models as computationally unbounded; they ask what classes of decision problems can be solved by humans interacting with models.
title: Building on the [ICA18] interactive-proof analogy to argue critiques are natural assistance
